title: Psalm 109:1–31
context: A psalm of David. In this imprecatory lament, David asks the God of his praise not to stay silent while lying mouths and groundless hatred repay his love with accusation. He gives himself to prayer and then asks for justice in kind against a cruel accuser who would not show kindness and loved to curse. He turns to ask God to act for his name’s sake and his loving kindness, confesses his poverty and the scorn he bears, and ends in thanks, because God stands beside the needy to save him from those who condemn him.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Psalm 109:1–31.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English editions of the sources named. Both camps take imprecatory speech seriously.

arminian.quote: God—the author and matter of all my praises. Adversaries—they requite my love with enmity. A wicked man—who will rule him with rigour and cruelty. Satan—to accuse him; for this was the place and posture of accusers in the Jewish courts. Sin—because it is not from his heart. Delighted not—in desiring and promoting the welfare of others. Garment—which a man wears constantly. That speak evil against my soul—with design to take away my life. Is good—above the mercy of all the creatures. The psalmist flees to prayer, asks just judgment on the merciless, and casts deliverance on the goodness of God’s mercy for His name’s sake.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Psalm 109)

reformed.quote: O God of my praise—David entrusts to God the vindication of his innocence when calumny is rampant; be not silent. On account of my love they opposed me; but I gave myself to prayer, not rendering evil for evil. When he forms maledictions he is not instigated by immoderate carnal propensity, nor by zeal without knowledge, nor by private personal considerations; he breathes under the Holy Spirit as God’s messenger. Yet leave room for grace—today’s enemy may become a friend—while the finally cruel deserve just judgment. Undertake for me for thy name’s sake; deliver because thy mercy is good—not for merit. He stands at the right hand of the poor to deliver his soul from those who condemn him to death.
reformed.source: Commentary on the Book of Psalms (on Psalm 109)

verses.text: God of my praise, don’t remain silent,
verses.arminianNotes:
God of my praise, don’t remain silent. Wesley: God—the author and matter of all my praises. Silence from God would leave the calumniated without a vindicator.

Both camps take the cry seriously. The psalmist asks the God he praises to speak. Imprecation later sits inside this appeal to the God of praise—not outside mercy’s frame.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: O God of my praise—David entrusts to God the vindication of his innocence when calumny is rampant. Be not silent: when the wicked asperse, it would be improper for the witness of innocence to remain silent. He represents Christ and the church under unjust hatred.

Appeal to God alone as defender. The imprecatory psalm begins with praise’s God, not with private spite.

verses.text: for they have opened the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit against me. They have spoken to me with a lying tongue.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wicked and deceitful mouths opened; lying tongues. The assault is verbal poison—fraud dressed as charge.

Both traditions share this lament over the wound that lies inflict. The righteous may be falsely accused; the answer is still prayer to God, not matching deceit.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the mouth of the wicked and of deceit are opened; false tongues surround him so that the ignorant may think the charge plausible.

Satan heaps calumny to tarnish the godly. Shared—take lying tongues as warfare; flee to God, not to counter-lies.

verses.text: They have also surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without a cause.
verses.arminianNotes:
Words of hate encircle; attack without cause. Wesley’s frame: love repaid with enmity.

Causeless hatred is named honestly. Both camps refuse to excuse the attackers or to pretend the hurt is unreal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: encompassed with words of hatred, fought without cause—harder to endure than a great army. What was prefigured in David is fulfilled in Christ; believers fill up what remains of His afflictions.

Shared suffering with Christ under causeless hate. The church is not surprised by verbal siege.

verses.text: In return for my love, they are my adversaries; but I am in prayer.
verses.arminianNotes:
In return for love they accuse; but I am in prayer. Wesley: Adversaries—they requite my love with enmity.

Love met by accusation, answered by prayer. Shared—both camps honor prayer instead of revenge as the first move. What comes through is a free choice to pray when accused; grace enables, the will still turns to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: on account of my love they opposed me; but I gave myself to prayer—not rendering evil for evil, but committing himself into God’s hand. The Spirit restrains so that the godly betake themselves by prayer to God alone.

Prayer is the Spirit’s restraint from revenge. Shared—love repaid with hate is answered at God’s tribunal.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse revenge as the first answer to false accusation and both honor prayer. Arminians emphasize the living turn to prayer when love is repaid with hate. Reformed readers stress Calvin’s point that the Spirit restrains the godly so they commit the case to God rather than seize fraudulent means.

verses.text: They have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love.
verses.arminianNotes:
The moral inversion is complete—good answered by evil.

Both share the psalmist’s outrage at injustice. The psalm will ask for judicial answer; it does not deny the goodness that was shown.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they rendered evil for good and hatred for love. Kindness to enemies makes their hate the more unnatural; Satan’s captivity of hearts is awful.

Document the wrong before God. The record of good for evil prepares the later appeal for just reward.

verses.text: Set a wicked man over him. Let an adversary stand at his right hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Set a wicked man over him. Let an adversary stand at his right hand. Wesley: A wicked man—who will rule him with rigour; Satan—to accuse him, as accusers stood in Jewish courts.

Imprecation begins—read as plea for judicial reciprocity under God, not as a license for personal vendetta. Wesleyan Arminians take the ask seriously: the accuser should meet an accuser, while believers do not turn the psalm into a charm of hate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: set a wicked person over him; let the adversary stand at his right hand. David is not driven by carnal spite, selfish interest, or zeal without knowledge; he speaks as God’s messenger under the Spirit. Believers must leave room for grace—today’s enemy may become tomorrow’s friend—yet the finally cruel deserve just judgment.

Weigh the three guards Calvin names. Imprecation is serious; it is neither rented cursing nor a shrug that God never judges.
verses.keyContrast: Both take the imprecation as serious appeal for just judgment, not as private spite. Arminians typically emphasize Wesley’s court imagery—rigorous reckoning for the cruel accuser—while refusing to live by curse. Calvinists stress Calvin’s guards: not selfish revenge, not carnal zeal, yet punishment for the obstinately cruel, with room left for God’s grace to convert.

verses.text: When he is judged, let him come out guilty. Let his prayer be turned into sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let his prayer be turned into sin. Wesley: Sin—because it is not from his heart.

Empty prayer from an unrepentant mouth does not avail. Shared—both camps know God is not mocked by religious words covering cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: when judged, let him depart guilty; let his prayer be turned into sin—either before earthly judges who disregard sham pleas, or before God to whom the wicked’s sacrifices are abomination.

Hypocritical prayer aggravates guilt. Shared refusal to treat pious talk as cover for oppression.

verses.text: Let his days be few. Let another take his office.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let his days be few. Let another take his office. Cited in Acts 1:20 of Judas.

Office can be stripped; life is not a blank check for the cruel. Acts reads this line of the betrayer. Both camps receive the apostle’s use.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: brevity of days as mark of disapprobation; another receives his office. Peter applies this to Judas (Acts 1:20). Temporary evils may touch the godly too, yet God sometimes displays marked judgment on the ungodly.

Shared apostolic reading toward Judas. The line comforts the church that lofty office without piety will fall.

verses.text: Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow. Heavy words—consequences cascading through a household.

Both camps feel the weight. The psalm targets a persecutor whose cruelty deserves covenant sanctions, not a call for believers to harm families. Wesleyan Arminians stress that such pleas are surrendered to God’s justice, not executed by private hands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the malediction extends to wife and children, depending on the brevity of life already named; Scripture sometimes visits iniquity across generations while never licensing personal cruelty.

Leave the severity with God the Judge. Do not soften the text into sentiment, and do not weaponize it for spite.

verses.text: Let his children be wandering beggars. Let them be sought from their ruins.
verses.arminianNotes:
Children wander and beg from ruins. Wesley: Desolate places—into which they fled for fear and shame.

The picture is desolation after judgment. Shared gravity—poverty here is judicial outcome in the psalm’s plea, not a program for the church to inflict.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: children wander without settled habitation, beggars seeking food from waste places. The severity matches the magnitude of guilt against the poor and brokenhearted named later.

Read the cascade as prophetic justice language, then practice mercy toward actual orphans you meet.

verses.text: Let the creditor seize all that he has. Let strangers plunder the fruit of his labor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Creditor seize all; strangers plunder his toil. Wesley: Catch—ensnare, by oppression and cunning; stranger—no right to his goods.

Wealth got or kept in cruelty is not safe. Shared—economic undoing is part of the pleaded judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the extortioner seizes all; strangers spoil his labor—poverty overtakes children of one who amassed by wrong.

God can strip unrighteous gain. Shared warning to oppressors who trust their estate.

verses.text: Let there be no one to extend kindness to him, neither let there be anyone to have pity on his fatherless children.
verses.arminianNotes:
None to extend kindness; none to have pity on his fatherless children.

The plea asks that the merciless find no mercy—measure for measure. Both camps teach Christians to show kindness widely; this verse is judicial speech about a particular cruel man, not a blank ethic of hardness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: none prolonging mercy to him or pitying his fatherless—those who were unmerciful justly find hard hearts around them (cf. Deut). David speaks as God’s messenger, not from private anguish alone.

Hardening of others’ pity can be judgment. Shared—do not confuse this plea with a command to withhold mercy from the needy you can help.

verses.text: Let his posterity be cut off. In the generation following let their name be blotted out.
verses.arminianNotes:
Posterity cut off; name blotted in the second generation.

Extinction of the name is ultimate earthly judgment. Both camps take the severity seriously—neither soft on evil nor eager for blood.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: posterity cut off; name effaced in the next generation—ruin so complete that the house does not rise again. Heavier than brief affliction.

Tremble at severity; improve it as reverence, not as a script for personal feuds.

verses.text: Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered by the LORD. Don’t let the sin of his mother be blotted out.
verses.arminianNotes:
Iniquity of fathers remembered; mother’s sin not blotted out.

Generational language is biblical and weighty. Personal responsibility (Ezek 18) stands together with corporate patterns of sin. Both camps confess God just.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: remember the iniquity of fathers and mothers so condemnation is complete—punishing to the third and fourth while mercy runs to a thousand for those who love Him. God prepares vessels; we must not measure His secret judgments by finite minds.

Severity that fills with fear. Shared—God is just; sons are not punished as innocent props of a parent’s crime when they themselves walk the same path.

verses.text: Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off their memory from the earth;
verses.arminianNotes:
Let them be before the LORD continually; cut off their memory from the earth.

Memory cut off is the opposite of the righteous remembrance in Psalm 112. Shared—God’s court keeps the record until judgment lands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: let sins stay before Jehovah continually; cut off their memorial from the earth. Vengeance made manifest so the world acquiesces in God’s equity.

Shared desire that justice be public enough to teach the earth, not merely private satisfaction.

verses.text: because he didn’t remember to show kindness, but persecuted the poor and needy man, the broken in heart, to kill them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Because he didn’t remember kindness, but persecuted the poor, needy, and brokenhearted to put them to death. The reason clause—cruelty toward the helpless.

Both camps agree this grounds the imprecations. Hate of the brokenhearted is not a small fault. Neither tradition is indifferent to the poor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he forgot to show mercy; persecuted the afflicted and poor and sorrowful in heart to slay him. Cruelty against the helpless is cowardly; the Spirit denounces heavy punishment for it.

Pray for all who trouble you, desire salvation of all, yet freely appeal for God to cut off the finally impenitent. Shared—protect the poor; do not romanticize the oppressor.

verses.text: Yes, he loved cursing, and it came to him. He didn’t delight in blessing, and it was far from him.
verses.arminianNotes:
He loved cursing, and it came to him. He didn’t delight in blessing, and it was far. Wesley: Delighted not—in desiring and promoting others’ welfare.

What he loved returns. Shared—cursing as habit invites curse; blessing refused is far from him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: as he loved cursing, let it come; as he didn’t delight in blessing, let it be far. Machinations recoil on the head that loved mischief.

Love of curse summons its own harvest under God.

verses.text: He clothed himself also with cursing as with his garment. It came into his inward parts like water, like oil into his bones.
verses.arminianNotes:
Clothed with cursing as a coat; soak like water and oil into bones. Wesley: Garment—worn constantly; water in the belly—near death; oil in bones—destroys.

Curse as clothing becomes inward poison. Shared vividness—do not sanitize the imagery or use it as a spell.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: clothed with cursing as a garment; let it come as water into bowels and oil into bones—cleaving, enveloping, penetrating.

The wicked man’s chosen coat becomes his judgment. Shared—read as prophetic justice, practice blessing with your own tongue.

verses.text: Let it be to him as the clothing with which he covers himself, for the belt that is always around him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Like a garment he wraps; like a belt every day.

The curse has become a daily habit, worn like clothing. Shared—sin worn as uniform is not a moment’s slip.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: mantle and girdle continually—cursing as constant dress.

Habit deepens judgment. Shared warning against making malice one’s everyday belt.

verses.text: This is the reward of my adversaries from the LORD, of those who speak evil against my soul.
verses.arminianNotes:
May this is the reward of my adversaries from the LORD, of those who speak evil against my soul. Wesley: That speak evil against my soul—with design to take away my life.

The reward is from the LORD—not from the psalmist’s knife. Shared handover of vengeance to God (cf. Rom 12). God does pay wages of sin; discernment still guards against rash personal malice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: let this be the work/reward from Jehovah of those hostile to me. David did not utter curses unadvisedly but as the Spirit dictated; he depends on God alone when the world frowns.

Reward from the LORD. Shared—accusers who seek a life are left to God’s payday.
verses.keyContrast: Both locate the reward with the LORD, not with private retaliation. Arminians press handing the case to God’s justice while refusing to live by curse. Calvin’s heirs generally underline Spirit-guided imprecation against the reprobate persecutor, still warning against rash personal malice.

verses.text: But deal with me, GOD the Lord, for your name’s sake, because your loving kindness is good, deliver me;
verses.arminianNotes:
But deal with me, GOD the Lord, for your name’s sake, because your loving kindness is good, deliver me. Wesley: Is good—above the mercy of all the creatures.

The turn of the psalm—from imprecation to plea on the name and hesed. Shared center: deliverance for God’s name and because mercy is good, not because the speaker is flawless.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: undertake for me for thy name’s sake; deliver because thy mercy is good. David does not plead merit; free grace and mercy are the ground. Even Christ’s human nature depended on the Father’s good pleasure; how much more we.

Name and mercy, not desert. Shared gospel logic inside an imprecatory psalm.

verses.text: for I am poor and needy. My heart is wounded within me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Poor and needy; heart stricken within.

The psalmist is honest about his weakness. Shared—poverty of spirit and stricken heart are the posture that seeks deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: poor and needy; heart wounded within. Outward affliction without humility is useless; God is physician to those who send up sighs, not to the hardened.

Publish your poverty before God; do not hide the stricken heart.

verses.text: I fade away like an evening shadow. I am shaken off like a locust.
verses.arminianNotes:
Gone like a shadow at evening; shaken off like a locust.

Frailty confessed. Shared—life feels brief and driven; that drives prayer, not despair alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: like a shadow when it declines; tossed as the locust—no settled place, incessant persecution.

The church’s unsettled path under trial. Shared comfort that God knows the shadow’s length.

verses.text: My knees are weak through fasting. My body is thin and lacks fat.
verses.arminianNotes:
Knees weak through fasting; body gaunt.

His grief and discipline show in his body. Shared—fasting and gauntness can mark earnest plea, not theatrical holiness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: knees feeble through fasting; flesh fails of fatness—sorrow and abstinence, or want in flight.

Shared realism about the body’s share in lament.

verses.text: I have also become a reproach to them. When they see me, they shake their head.
verses.arminianNotes:
Object of scorn; they wag their heads.

The shame is public. Shared link to other passion psalms—scorn does not prove God has abandoned the cause.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: became a reproach; they shake the head—insolence toward the afflicted and toward faith itself.

Scorn as temptation; hold the warnings of the law without concluding you are cast off forever.

verses.text: Help me, LORD, my God. Save me according to your loving kindness;
verses.arminianNotes:
Help me, LORD, my God; save me according to your loving kindness!

Bare cry—help and save by hesed. Shared—steadfast love is the measure of salvation asked.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: help me; save according to thy mercy—repeat the prayer under delay and slander. Desire deliverance that manifests God’s glory, not mere self-safety.

Mercy as the rule of help. Shared insistence that God’s hand be seen.

verses.text: that they may know that this is your hand; that you, LORD, have done it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Let them know this is your hand; that you, LORD, have done it!

Public theodicy—enemies must recognize God’s act. Shared—salvation that silences boast in human rescue.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they shall know this is thy hand—special display so the ungodly cannot open their mouths. Point to God’s hand only if your own mind has recognized it.

Glory of God in deliverance outranks private relief alone.

verses.text: They may curse, but you bless. When they arise, they will be shamed, but your servant shall rejoice.
verses.arminianNotes:
They may curse, but you bless. When they arise and are put to shame; your servant will be glad.

Curse versus blessing—God’s blessing outweighs human curse. Shared confidence for the servant who stays under mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: they shall curse, but thou shalt bless; when they arise they shall be ashamed; thy servant shall rejoice. Relying on grace, David sets their malice at nought.

Blessing from God nullifies curse from men. Shared joy of the servant under that blessing.

verses.text: Let my adversaries be clothed with dishonor. Let them cover themselves with their own shame as with a robe.
verses.arminianNotes:
Accusers clothed with dishonor; themselves with their own shame as a cloak.

Shame as garment mirrors the curse-coat of v. 18. Shared poetic justice—dishonor fits those who sought another’s death.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: adversaries clothed with shame and covered with confusion as a garment.

Look beyond present lofty airs of the ungodly to the shame God will wrap them in.

verses.text: I will give great thanks to the LORD with my mouth. Yes, I will praise him among the multitude.
verses.arminianNotes:
Great thanks with my mouth; praise in the midst of the throng.

Vowed public praise after deliverance. Shared—thanksgiving belongs in the assembly, not only in private relief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: praise Jehovah greatly with the mouth in the assembly of the great/many—public acknowledgment from the heart’s bottom.

Tongue united with heart for mutual edification. Shared return of praise to the throng.

verses.text: For he will stand at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those who judge his soul.
verses.arminianNotes:
For he will stand at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those who judge his soul to death.

Climax—God at the needy’s right hand (contrast the accuser at the wicked’s right hand in v. 6). Shared gospel shape: the needy are saved from soul-condemners. Both camps end in comfort for the poor in spirit, not in celebration of cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: God stands at the right hand of the poor to deliver his soul from condemnations—present even when He seemed far. Judges of his life were formidable; God still saved.

The needy one’s advocate is God Himself. Shared—imprecation’s end is salvation of the condemned innocent, not a hobby of hate.
verses.keyContrast: Both end with God at the needy one’s right hand to save from death-dealing condemnation—the structural answer to the accuser at the wicked’s right hand (v. 6). Arminians stress the open comfort for every needy one who cries to this God of praise and mercy. Reformed readers commonly emphasize God’s sure defense of His afflicted poor against condemning powers, the God who justly answers the finally cruel.
